title: Seventy-eight years, 32 moments
lede: From a baby furniture store in Washington to pop-up shops in malls, with the money and the rivals alongside. Filter by thread.

events.title: Children’s Bargain Town
events.text: Charles Lazarus, 25, opens a baby furniture store in Washington, D.C.

events.title: The Toys “R” Us name
events.text: Lazarus opens a store that sells only toys, run like a supermarket, with a backward R on the sign.

events.title: Geoffrey the giraffe
events.text: The mascot, descended from an earlier character called Dr. G. Raffe, takes his name. His first TV commercial airs in 1973.

events.title: Sold to Interstate Stores
events.text: Lazarus sells his four toy supermarkets for $7.5M and stays on to run them.

events.title: The parent goes bankrupt
events.text: Interstate files for bankruptcy. There are 51 Toys “R” Us stores, and more open during the reorganization.

events.title: Toys “R” Us, Inc.
events.text: Interstate emerges with 63 toy stores, takes the Toys “R” Us name and is led by Lazarus as a public company.

events.title: $1 billion in sales
events.text: Sales reach $1.3B. The first Kids “R” Us clothing stores open. Stores in Canada and Singapore follow in 1984.

events.title: Peak share, and Walmart arrives
events.text: Toys “R” Us holds 25.4% of U.S. toy sales. Walmart, at 9.5%, begins using hot toys as loss leaders.

events.title: Lazarus steps down
events.text: The founder hands the chief executive’s job to Michael Goldstein.

events.title: Babies “R” Us
events.text: The first three baby superstores open.

events.title: toysrus.com
events.text: The company starts selling online. Its share of U.S. toy sales has fallen to 18.4% (1997).

events.title: Walmart is the largest toy seller
events.text: Walmart passes Toys “R” Us in U.S. toy sales. That Christmas some toysrus.com orders arrive late.

events.title: The Amazon alliance
events.text: A ten-year agreement makes Amazon the exclusive online outlet for Toys “R” Us, for a base fee of $50M a year plus a share of sales.

events.title: Times Square flagship
events.text: A 110,000-square-foot store opens in New York with a 60-foot indoor Ferris wheel.

events.title: Suing Amazon
events.text: The company sues to enforce its exclusivity rights. Amazon counterclaims in June.

events.title: Strategic review
events.text: The board says it will pursue separating the toy business from Babies “R” Us and may sell the toy business.

events.title: Merger agreement
events.text: Bain Capital, KKR and Vornado agree to buy the whole company for $26.75 a share.

events.title: The buyout closes
events.text: A $6.6B merger takes the company private. By January 2006 total indebtedness is $5,947M and 87 U.S. toy stores are slated to close.

events.title: Court severs the Amazon deal
events.text: New Jersey Superior Court Judge Margaret Mary McVeigh rules that Amazon breached the agreement. No damages are awarded.

events.title: Buying up the fallen
events.text: The company acquires FAO Schwarz in May and the KB Toys brand in September. On July 21 Amazon pays $51M to settle.

events.title: IPO filed
events.text: An S-1 proposes an offering of up to $800M, mainly to repay debt. Total indebtedness is $5,196M.

events.title: IPO withdrawn
events.text: The company says it has “determined not to pursue” the offering “at this time.” Fiscal 2013 ends with a net loss of $1.04B.

events.title: Times Square closes
events.text: The company declines to renew the flagship lease, citing “meaningful rent savings.”

events.title: FAO Schwarz sold
events.text: The brand goes to ThreeSixty Group. Terms are not disclosed.

events.title: Chapter 11
events.text: Toys “R” Us and certain subsidiaries file in the Eastern District of Virginia, with about $4.9B of debt.

events.title: Wind-down announced
events.text: The company seeks court approval to liquidate all 735 U.S. stores.

events.title: Charles Lazarus dies
events.text: The founder dies at 94, a week after the announcement.

events.title: Last U.S. stores close
events.text: More than 30,000 workers are left looking for work.

events.title: The lenders keep the name; the workers get a fund
events.text: The trademark auction is cancelled in October. On November 20, KKR and Bain Capital announce a $20M hardship fund.

events.title: Two small stores
events.text: Tru Kids opens stores of about 6,000 square feet in Paramus, New Jersey, and Houston. Both close in January 2021.

events.title: WHP Global takes control
events.text: The brand manager acquires a controlling interest in Tru Kids. A flagship opens at American Dream that December.

events.title: 120 stores for the holidays
events.text: WHP Global and Go! Retail Group announce 120 U.S. stores, many small and temporary.
